children: Saudi Arabia could exhaust oil inventories available for export within days unless it restarts a critical pipeline to the Red Sea, potentially removing as much as 4% of global supply from an already strained market, Reuters reported.

Drone attacks forced the kingdom to shut its east-west pipeline on Friday. The route has carried about 4 million barrels a day across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing Saudi exports to bypass the war-disrupted Strait of Hormuz.

Industry sources cited by Reuters offered conflicting estimates for repairs. One said the work could require five to six weeks, while another suggested limited operations might resume sooner. Saudi officials have not disclosed the extent of the damage or provided a timetable.

Yanbu reportedly has enough oil stored to maintain exports for another five to seven days. Saudi Arabia also holds supplies at Egypt’s Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir terminals, but those inventories are limited and cannot replace continuing pipeline deliveries indefinitely.

The outage comes after Saudi production fell to 6.2 million barrels a day in August, compared with 10.9 million in February. The International Energy Agency expects global supply to contract by 5.7 million barrels a day this year as regional disruptions persist.

Before the war, the Middle East supplied roughly 22 million barrels a day. Shipments through Hormuz have since fallen to an estimated 6 million to 9 million barrels a day. Risks increased further Friday when Houthi forces seized an island near the entrance to the Red Sea.

A prolonged pipeline shutdown could drive crude and fuel prices still higher, intensifying inflation and reducing the likelihood of interest-rate cuts. Energy producers and oil-service companies may benefit, while airlines, transportation companies, manufacturers and consumer businesses face higher costs. Bond and equity markets also could come under pressure if another inflation shock pushes Treasury yields higher.

title: Saudi pipeline outage threatens 4% of global oil supply
